20503-the-nation-s-river-a-report-on-the:
The Nation's River is a United States Department of the Interior report on the Potomac River. The Potomac flows past the capital, and the report treats it as a national trust. It studies the river's pollution, banks, and public use.

To protect the mainstem Potomac and its banks from Washington to Cumberland, Maryland, the report urges quick action. It calls for legislative authorization, funding, and a Potomac national river area open to the public. The report shows the conservation thinking of its time: a great river near a great city should belong to everyone.
20629-torchy-as-a-pa:
Torchy as a Pa, published in 1919, makes Sewell Ford's slangy hero a father. Torchy greets fatherhood the way he greeted office work: fast talk first, feelings after. A card announcing the new arrival sets the comedy going.

He picks the card on the fly and reads the neat script on it. At home after September 15, it says, at an address on West Hundred and Umpty-Umpt Street. Hamilton Porter Blake, anyway? Torchy demands, missing the point as usual. The book follows him through babies, in-laws, and the Corrugated Trust, in the series' longest-running vein of fun.
21499-europe-whither-bound-quo-vadis-eur:
Stephen Graham asks where Europe is heading in Europe, Whither Bound?, letters from the capitals of 1921. The book came out in 1922, after the letters ran in Country Life. Graham made no deep study of each land; he kept the taxi waiting, as he jokes.

That speed is the point: he wanted Europe seen whole, as one body. Pride of Christian culture before 1914 now faced, he feared, decline and death. Bishops, editors, and officers helped him on his rapid tour. Few travel books so soon after the Great War tried to grasp the continent entire.
23072-the-voyage-of-the-steadfast-the-yo:
W. H. G. Kingston sounds a wreck alarm in The Voyage of the Steadfast. Hannah cries out at a gun flash near the dark rocks offshore. A second flash follows. Some unfortunate ship, she is sure, is signaling from the reef, perhaps already wrecked on it.

The Steadfast carries young missionaries toward the Pacific, and storm, wreck, and rescue test their calling early. Kingston wrote sea adventure with a missionary heart, filling the Pacific with converts, dangers, and providence. His books shaped British boys' picture of the ocean world. This voyage shows his whole method, a gun flash in the dark, a boat launched into surf, and faith keeping stroke with the oars.
a-mountain-europa:
John Fox Jr. sets his tale in the high Kentucky Cumberlands, the country of his famous feud stories. A young woman of the mountains, Europa, grows up where family honor is guarded with rifles and where a stranger from the lowlands is watched with suspicion. Her beauty and spirit draw notice beyond her valley.

Fox follows her through the pressures of mountain custom, courtship, and the old quarrels that rule men's lives around her. He writes the ridges, coves, and fiddle music of the region with the affection that made him the Cumberlands' best-known novelist. The story is a romance, but its weight lies in showing how completely the mountains shape the people born among them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambrogio-fopp:
Ambrogio Foppa, generally called Caradosso, was an Italian goldsmith, sculptor, and die sinker, born at Mondonico near Como, or Pavia by other accounts, in 1445. He died about 1527. His Christian name may have been Cristoforo, not Ambrogio. He served Lodovico il Moro of Milan, making a fine medal and goldsmith's pieces, then worked in Rome for Julius II and Leo X.

Cellini called him the most excellent goldsmith of his time, without equal in dies, citing his Rome medal showing Bramante and his St. Peter's design. He is credited with San Satiro's sacristy terra-cotta reliefs, nearly Donatello's equal in beauty, and with medals of Julius II, Francesco Sforza, and Gian Giacomo Trivulzio. Many Italian church sacristies hold goldsmith work attributed to him, especially reliquaries, morses, and crosiers, plus a papal mitre for Julius II.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arequipa:
Arequipa, suffragan of the archdiocese of Lima in Peru, was erected by Gregory XIII on 15 April 1577 at Philip II's request. Philip had sought three Peruvian dioceses under royal patronage. Its population in 1901 was 35,000, and it holds a cathedral honouring the Assumption of the Virgin, a Jesuit college, an infirmary, and several convents. Arequipa is Peru's second city, near the volcanic Andean peak called Misti.

In 1868 earthquake shocks destroyed most of its buildings and killed 6,000 people. The city was founded by Pizarro. The entry is a compact diocesan sketch, joining church institutions to civic disaster. It shows a colonial foundation, a cathedral city under a volcano, and a community rebuilt after a quake that levelled most of what it had built.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-atahuallpa:
Atahuallpa, properly Atau-Huallpa, a name usually derived from huallpa, some native bird, was son of the Inca war leader Huayna Capac and a woman from Quito. Hence, descent running in the female line, he was not an Inca but an Indian of Ecuador. Long wars in which Incas overpowered Ecuadorian tribes brought permanent Inca war parties to Ecuador, mixing Inca men with Quito women and children into a new tribe.

Collisions followed between that tribe and descendants of Inca women, with Atau-Huallpa leading the former and Huascar, duly elected war chief at Cuzco, leading the latter. Atau-Huallpa behaved with great cruelty, nearly exterminating resisting Ecuadorian tribes, finally prevailed, and sent warriors south along the mountain spine against Cuzco. When Pizarro landed at Tumbez on Peru's northern coast in 1532, the Quito-Cuzco struggle shaped the conquest that followed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chilapa: A short entry on the Diocese of Chilapa in Mexico, suffragan to the Archdiocese of Mexico and covering the southern state of Guerrero. Created in 1863, it has had three bishops: Ambrosio Serrano, Ramon Ibarra, and Homobono Anaya. Its population, counted as entirely Catholic, stands at 361,239 souls, served by 64 parishes and 94 priests. Chilapa, the episcopal city, lies about 125 miles south-west of Mexico City and held 8,256 people in 1895.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-clemens-non-p:
Clemens non Papa, whose true name was Jacques Clement, represented the sixteenth-century Flemish or Netherland school of music and died in 1558. The one certain fact of his life: he preceded Nicolas Gombert as Charles the Fifth's court choirmaster. His nickname non Papa means not the Pope. It distinguished him from the contemporary Pope Clement the Seventh, who reigned from 1523 to 1534.

His style stays always noble and fluent. Yet he shows his school's fault: contrapuntal forms elaborated at clear declamation's expense. Nevertheless he ranks among Palestrina's and Orlandus Lassus's chief forerunners, overshadowed by them alone. His more important works include ten masses, for six, five, and four voices, published at Louvain from 1555 to 1580. They also include many motets and four volumes of Souter Liedekens, psalms set to familiar Netherland melodies, published at Antwerp in 1556 to 1557.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-auri: A 1913 entry on Aurispa — the Sicilian humanist. Edmund Burke honors his famous manuscripts. His pen brought the Greek codices. The Renaissance prized its Eastern lore. The Poggio of the manuscript hunt. His 1459 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hypaepa: This 1913 reference article on Hypaepa — the Lydian town, now a titular see. Sophrone Pétridès notes its storied past. Its bishops grace the old lists. The Church keeps its ancient name. A see of the Anatolian hills. Its bishops signed the ancient creeds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-santos-a: A 1913 entry on Atahualpa — the Andean rebel. Adolph Francis Bandelier unfolds his jungle rising. He defied the Spanish yoke. The mountains knew the daring name. The eighteenth century told his tale. His 1756 death is famed. His 1742 rising is famed. His 1742 jungle revolt is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lampa: A 1913 entry on Lampa — the ancient see. Sophrone Pétridès gives its ruined story. Its bishops served the Cretan flock. The entry keeps its modest record. A titular see today. Its ancient bishops are famed. Its titular rank is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maestro-di-ca: This 1913 reference piece on the Maestro di Camera — the papal chamberlain. Paul Maria Baumgarten unfolds his courtly lore. He orders the pontiff's household. Rome keeps the ancient office. The Vatican knows his name. Its 1907 study is famed. Its courtly office is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-monomotapa: Monomotapa was the great Shona kingdom of southeastern Africa, whose stone city of Great Zimbabwe awed Portuguese visitors. This entry covers its history, the Jesuit missions, and the martyrdom of Father Silveira. Gold, stone, and the cross in Africa: Portuguese traders sought its fabled wealth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sappa: Sappa, the name of the Albanian see, carries a Catholic history. This brief entry notes its bishops and its past. A quiet name from the Balkan hills: its old bishops served the flock in Albania's north in the mountains of the Dukagjin.

doe-osti-3625658-design-of-a-cryogenic-a: Quantum computers live at near absolute zero — and stray infrared light can wreck their qubits. Mailliard and Temples built a deep-cold test rig for comparing how different qubit packages leak infrared. The head-to-head points to packaging that keeps qubits cold and quiet.
govdocs-archive_org-PhysicalControlOfThe:
José M. R. Delgado was a Spanish-born brain researcher at Yale who spent his career testing whether behavior could be steered by electrical signals sent straight into the brain. His 1969 book sums up that work and argues that people stand close to a new age of control over their own minds.

Delgado describes his stimoceiver, a small radio device implanted in the brain that could trigger movements and moods at the push of a button. His best-known test stopped a charging bull in a ring with a radio signal. He closes by urging society to use such tools for mental liberation rather than fear them, a claim still argued over today.
govdocs-archive_org-TheFirstHolocaust-Je:
Don Heddesheimer wrote The First Holocaust as volume 6 of the Barnes Review's Holocaust Handbook Series. His subject is World War I-era Jewish fund-raising campaigns in America and the claims made in them about Jewish suffering in Europe.

Heddesheimer points to reports such as a 1919 New York Times item speaking of six million Jews, and argues that such figures were raised for fund-raising effect long before World War II. The book is revisionist history and is widely disputed by historians. It is held as an archive item, without endorsement, for readers studying that literature itself.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Preparation-Ear:
An editorial asks whether Watergate is ending, under the line 'Watergate: An End Is in Sight?' Its subject is Leon Jaworski, the special prosecutor. Jaworski was struggling to obtain 64 White House tapes from President Nixon. Nixon, for his part, was working to bring the scandal to an end on his own terms.

The tapes fight decided Watergate. A prosecutor subpoenaed recordings; a president claimed privilege; the courts would settle it. An editorial of that season shows how the struggle looked before the settlement: uncertain, procedural, and political at once. The piece preserves the press taking the nation's temperature mid-crisis, when the outcome that now seems fixed was still in doubt.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_mexico-a:
In September 2014, forty-three students from the Ayotzinapa teachers' college in Mexico vanished after attacks in Iguala. Kate Doyle and Claire Dorfman edited this briefing book, number 823, published in March 2023. It draws on the Guacamaya leaks, a large trove of hacked military files.

The leaks show Mexico's military had surveilled the Ayotzinapa school for years before the disappearance. Intelligence reports reveal a constant exchange of messages during the night of the attacks themselves. Yet the military continues to deny investigators complete access to its archives. The posting joins leaked proof of watching with official refusal to open the rest.
lippa:
Beatrice Kemp, writing as Beatrice Egerton, published this novel in London. Eden, Remington and Company issued it from King Street, Covent Garden. Chapter One opens at four o'clock on a deserted July street. Cab-drivers sleep while sentries swelter in their bearskins.

Jimmy Dalrymple confesses to his friend Chubby that he is nearly done. Heat and money troubles press on the young Guards officer. Chubby blames racing, and Jimmy calls him an ass. A Shakespeare epigraph frames life as a stage for every man. Jimmy serves in the Guards, readers learn from the club talk. Helmdon, better known as Chubby, lectures him on racing habits.
nasa-tm-19710011026-an-improved-method-f:
Charles L Zola of the Lewis Research Center published this method in February 1971. It tackles a payload problem for spacecraft that use electric propulsion at low power levels. Fitting less than the best power level can cut payload sharply. Zola asked whether a lighter spacecraft could recover some of that loss.

His answer was yes. For a given launcher, the best total spacecraft mass can sit below the most mass the launcher can inject. Trimming mass raises the payload share when electric power is scarce. Zola showed the method on a Mercury orbiter design. It used solar electric propulsion and a Titan Centaur launcher.
nasa-tm-19710019493-materials-technology:
R E Gluyas and A F Lietzke of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a June 1971 nuclear meeting in Boston. It lays out a materials program for a compact fast reactor meant to supply power in space. The fuel was uranium mononitride, clad in a tantalum alloy with a tungsten liner. Every material had to survive hot liquid lithium coolant.

One half of the program developed the factory process. It covers making the fuel, cladding, and finished fuel pins, plus inspection. The other half ran compatibility studies. Fuel had to suit its cladding and the coolant. The team also checked control drum and reflector materials. The goal was a fuel element ready for reactor service.
nasa-tm-19720020704-results-of-the-ballo:
The Goddard Space Flight Center issued these experiment results in March 1972, numbered X-524-72-125. The Balloon Atmospheric Propagation Experiment flew its first flights in 1970. Two laser beams climbed from the ground to receivers carried above most of the air. One beam was green argon light, and the other was infrared. Earth's atmosphere makes such beams twinkle and waver. The flights measured that shimmering, called scintillation, directly.

At the same time, instruments tracked the turbulence along the path. Matching the two records showed how air motion distorts laser light. Balloons lifted the receivers clear of the thickest air. The work served designers of laser links between ground and space. Its short name was BAPE 1, marking the first flight series.
podcast-tuckercarlson-aLtfKq08YpA:
Tucker Carlson gives a talk on the spiritual roots of America's political breakdown. He argues the crisis in public life is at base a crisis of faith. No guest joins him, so the episode is his case alone, made at length.

Carlson says a country that loses shared belief in God loses shared truth as well. He links that loss to rage in politics, broken homes, and a sense of drift. He also takes aim at leaders who mock faith while the country frays. Listeners get his full frame for the age in one place. Fans and critics alike can hear the claim as he states it.
the-curlytops-on-star-island-or-camping-: Howard R. Garis wrote The Curlytops on Star Island, or Camping Out with Grandpa, with pictures by Julia Greene. A series page dated 1918 lists the Curlytops books: At Cherry Farm, On Star Island, Snowed In, and At Uncle Frank's Ranch. The contents open with chapters called The Blue Light, What the Farmer Told, Off to Star Island, Overboard, The Bag of Salt, and Ted and the Bear. Only the front matter and the start of the contents are present here.
the-fotygraft-album-shown-to-the-new-nei:
Frank Wing drew and wrote The Fotygraft Album, shown to a new neighbor by Rebecca Sparks Peters, aged eleven. The book was printed at Chicago in 1915 and ran through seven printings in a year.

Rebecca greets Mrs. Miggs at the door while her mother is out borrowing thread, molasses, and eggs. She sits the guest down and turns the album pages, one kin folk at a time. Her mother as a girl wears real mink from Uncle Seth's store. Aunt Mary Jane is praised for jimpson-weed salve and peach preserves. Each photo brings a child's plain talk on kin, looks, and worth.
tom-swift-and-his-motor-boat-or-the-riva:
Victor Appleton opens with Mr. Barton Swift asking his son where he is going, as Tom pushes his motor-cycle toward the country road. Tom plainly has an object in view. Contents promise twenty-five chapters beginning at a motor-boat auction on Lake Carlopa, with lively bidding and a timely warning.

Tom and Andy clash repeatedly, the Arrow disappears, robbery news arrives, and a balloon catches fire before a rescue. Plans for an airship and a solved mystery lead to winning a race. Readers get an early Tom Swift adventure built around speed, rivals, and a father's watchful questions.
